newsitem.title: USA: Ending bacteria's drug resistance may be possible.
newsitem.headline: Ending bacteria's drug resistance may be possible.

text.p: It might be possible to make bacteria that resist antibiotic drugs, such as organisms that cause tuberculosis and meningitis, drug-sensitive again, scientists suggested on Monday.

Researchers using new technology managed to eliminate the material in strains of the common E. coli bacterium that prevents antibiotic drugs from working, according to a report in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

"Although the path from our experiments to a practical therapeutic tool may be a very long and costly one, this method could restore the full usefulness of today's front-line antibiotics, thus bypassing the tremendous expense of developing new antibiotics," the article's author, Sidney Altman, said in a statement.
The technology, using what are known as EGS oligozymes, is licensed by Innovir Laboratories Inc. of New York.

Innovir's chairman, Allan Goldberg, said this technology could offer an alternative to developing more powerful antibiotics, ultimately producing a treatment for people suffering from diseases caused by drug-resistant bacteria.
The problem of drug-resistant bacteria has meant that some diseases formerly thought to be under control, such as tuberculosis and meningitis, are reappearing.
This has happened because over time bacteria acquire traits that make them resistant to antibiotics, and the resistant genes are passed on to other bacteria, making antibiotics less effective.
